group.title: Scientific language
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: How thick a liquid is and how much it resists flowing.
examples: Honey has a much higher {viscosity} than water.
wrong: Water has more viscosity than honey, so it pours more slowly.

words.meaning: A measure of disorder in a system, which tends to increase over time.
examples: Left alone, a tidy room drifts toward {entropy}.
wrong: Entropy is the natural tendency of things to become more ordered.

words.meaning: To break down slowly into simpler parts, especially after death.
examples: Leaves {decompose} into rich soil over the winter.
wrong: The plastic decomposed in a week and then stayed in the sea for centuries.

words.meaning: Not reacting chemically with other substances; not moving.
examples: Helium is an {inert} gas.
wrong: The gas is inert, so it explodes when it touches anything.

words.meaning: A form of a chemical element with a different number of neutrons.
examples: Carbon-14 is a radioactive {isotope} used in dating fossils.
wrong: An isotope is a totally different element with a new name.

words.meaning: A close relationship between two living things that helps both.
examples: Bees and flowers live in {symbiosis}.
wrong: Their symbiosis harmed both species and helped neither.

words.meaning: The body’s way of keeping its inner conditions stable.
examples: Sweating helps maintain {homeostasis} in hot weather.
wrong: Homeostasis makes body temperature swing wildly all day.

words.meaning: The slow movement of water through a thin layer from a weak solution to a strong one; gradual absorption.
examples: Plant roots take up water by {osmosis}.
wrong: She learned the language by osmosis, through hours of strict grammar drills.

words.meaning: The time it takes for half of a substance to decay or disappear.
examples: This isotope has a {half-life} of about 5,700 years.
wrong: The half-life is the time it takes a substance to double.

words.meaning: To spread or travel through a material; also to make plants grow from parent plants.
examples: Sound waves {propagate} faster through water than through air.
wrong: The wave propagated by stopping completely at the wall.

words.meaning: To give someone a weak form of a disease to protect them from it.
examples: Children are {inoculated} against measles.
wrong: They inoculated the cattle so that the disease would spread faster.

words.meaning: The chemical process of burning.
examples: Car engines run on the {combustion} of fuel.
wrong: Combustion happens when a fire is put out with water.

words.meaning: The distance between two wave peaks; also a way of thinking you share with someone.
examples: Red light has a longer {wavelength} than blue light.
wrong: A wavelength is the speed at which a car travels.

words.meaning: Moving or pushing away from the center of something that spins.
examples: {Centrifugal} force presses you against the wall of the spinning ride.
wrong: Centrifugal force pulls a spinning object in toward its center.

words.meaning: Relating to movement or produced by movement.
examples: A rolling ball has {kinetic} energy.
wrong: Kinetic energy is the energy an object has when it is completely still.

words.meaning: To spread out and disappear gradually.
examples: The fog {dissipated} by noon.
wrong: The heat dissipated and grew stronger in one spot.

words.meaning: Letting liquids or gases pass through.
examples: Sandy soil is highly {permeable}.
wrong: The wall is permeable, so no water can get through it.

words.meaning: Able to slowly destroy metal or other materials by chemical action; harmful.
examples: Seawater is {corrosive} to steel.
wrong: The acid is corrosive, so it makes metal stronger.

words.meaning: Able to dissolve in a liquid.
examples: Sugar is {soluble} in water.
wrong: Sand is soluble, so it vanishes as soon as it touches water.

words.meaning: To move back and forth regularly; to keep changing between two states.
examples: The pendulum {oscillates} every two seconds.
wrong: The needle oscillated by staying perfectly still.

words.meaning: To bend light or sound as it passes from one material into another.
examples: Water {refracts} light, so a straw looks bent.
wrong: The glass refracted the light by letting it pass in a perfectly straight line.

words.meaning: A substance that can cause cancer.
examples: Tobacco smoke contains many known {carcinogens}.
wrong: A carcinogen is a vitamin that protects you from cancer.

words.meaning: A germ, such as a virus or bacterium, that causes disease.
examples: Boiling water kills most {pathogens}.
wrong: A pathogen is a helpful germ that cures diseases.

words.meaning: The starting assumption in a study that there is no real effect or difference.
examples: The data let us reject the {null hypothesis}.
wrong: The null hypothesis claims that the new drug has a huge effect.

words.meaning: The science of naming and sorting living things into groups; any system of classification.
examples: The {taxonomy} places whales among mammals, not fish.
wrong: A taxonomy is a list that puts things in no order at all.

words.meaning: A difference of about ten times in size or amount.
examples: The new chip is an {order of magnitude} faster.
wrong: An order of magnitude means a tiny change of about one percent.

words.meaning: The bending of light or sound as it passes from one substance into another.
examples: {Refraction} makes a straw look bent in a glass of water.
wrong: Refraction keeps light moving in a perfectly straight line through water.

words.meaning: The process plants use to make food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.
examples: Leaves turn sunlight into energy through {photosynthesis}.
wrong: Photosynthesis is how animals digest their food at night.

words.meaning: To change in form or nature, especially through a change in genes.
examples: The virus {mutated} quickly, so the old vaccine stopped working.
wrong: The cells mutated, so they stayed exactly the same as before.

words.meaning: Growing faster and faster, by multiplying again and again.
examples: The virus showed {exponential} growth.
wrong: Exponential growth is slow and steady, adding the same amount each year.

words.meaning: The speed of something in a given direction.
examples: The rocket reached a {velocity} of 11 kilometers per second.
wrong: Velocity measures how heavy an object is.

words.meaning: To suggest an idea as a possible explanation that still needs testing.
examples: Researchers {hypothesize} that sleep helps memory.
wrong: She hypothesized the result after it had been fully proven.

words.meaning: A statement in mathematics that can be proved by reasoning.
examples: The {theorem} was finally proved after three centuries.
wrong: A theorem is a guess that nobody can ever prove.

words.meaning: Able to be shown false by a test or observation.
examples: A scientific claim must be {falsifiable}.
wrong: The theory is falsifiable, so no test could ever disprove it.

words.meaning: A hidden factor that affects the results of a study and may give a false link.
examples: Age was a {confounding variable} in the diet study.
wrong: A confounding variable has no effect at all on the results.

words.meaning: A protein that speeds up chemical reactions in living things.
examples: An {enzyme} in saliva begins to break down food.
wrong: Enzymes are rocks found deep inside the earth.

words.meaning: To make a liquid weaker by adding water or another liquid; to weaken.
examples: {Dilute} the juice with an equal amount of water.
wrong: She diluted the syrup by boiling away all the water.

words.meaning: Related so that when one amount rises, the other falls at the same rate.
examples: Pressure is {inversely proportional} to volume.
wrong: The two amounts are inversely proportional, so both rise together.

words.meaning: Sand, soil or other matter that settles at the bottom of a liquid.
examples: A layer of {sediment} built up on the riverbed.
wrong: The sediment floated to the top and stayed there.

words.meaning: Done again and again, improving a little each time.
examples: Design is an {iterative} process.
wrong: The process was iterative, so they did it once and never repeated it.
